RICE scoring

Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort — what the formula actually buys you, and the four places it quietly misleads.

1. A Tuesday in Bengaluru

On the morning of 14 October 2025, Meghna Rau had thirty-four candidate items on a whiteboard and room in the quarter for perhaps nine of them. Rau was VP of Product at Nihaar Retail Cloud, a nine-year-old company in Bengaluru whose billing, inventory and loyalty software ran the tills of 5,800 supermarket outlets belonging to 240 regional chains — the kind of two-hundred-store business that is too large for a spreadsheet and too small to build its own systems. Three engineering squads, roughly nineteen person-months of capacity for the December quarter, and a board that had asked for one number to improve: net revenue retention, which had drifted from 108 per cent to 101 over four quarters.

Two items dominated the room. Rohit Menon, the chief revenue officer, wanted an offline billing mode so that tills could keep ringing through internet outages; he had ₹4.2 crore of pipeline he said hung on it, and three named logos. Devika Nair, who ran support, wanted returns-and-exchange automation, because 31 per cent of her ticket volume in September had been store staff wrestling with returns by hand. Both were right in the sense that both were describing real pain. Both were also arguing from the strength of their own evidence, which is a different thing from arguing about the same evidence.

Rau had watched this meeting fail before. The pattern was familiar: the loudest well-prepared advocate wins, engineering absorbs the decision as a mandate rather than a judgement, and three months later nobody can reconstruct why the loser lost. What she wanted was not a better argument. It was a way to make the argument be about something checkable — so that when the ranking changed, everyone could see which assumption had moved. That is the job RICE was built to do.

2. The idea, stated precisely

RICE is a scoring method that converts a candidate piece of work into a single number by estimating four quantities and combining them in a fixed way:

Reach — how many units of the thing you care about (people, accounts, outlets, sessions, transactions) will encounter this change within a stated time window. Impact — how much the change moves a single named outcome metric for each unit it reaches, expressed on a coarse multiplier scale. Confidence — a percentage discount reflecting how much evidence sits behind the other three numbers. Effort — the total cost of building and shipping it, in person-months across every function involved, not just engineering.

The score is Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort. The units are, loosely, "expected outcome-weighted reach per person-month" — a rate, not a total. The method was developed at Intercom around 2016, by the product manager Sean McBride, and published on the company's blog; it spread quickly because it was a small, honest improvement on the value-versus-effort two-by-two that most teams were already drawing. Value-versus-effort asks you to plot items on a grid with "value" on one axis. RICE's contribution is to refuse the word value and force it apart into three separately arguable components — how many, how much each, and how sure are you.

The sentence Rau could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "RICE does not tell us what to build. It tells us which of our disagreements is actually load-bearing."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics look trivial and are not, because four of the steps are usually left implicit and every one of them is where the errors enter.

Fix the window first. Reach is meaningless without a period. Nihaar chose one quarter. The choice is not neutral: a quarterly window flatters items that hit everyone immediately and penalises items whose audience accumulates, such as a feature only new chains will adopt at onboarding. Rau's rule was that the window must be the same for every item in the list and must be stated on the sheet.

Fix the unit of reach. Nihaar counts outlets, not chains and not end shoppers. This matters enormously. Counting chains would have made the offline-billing case look small (twelve chains) and counting shoppers would have made it look enormous (roughly 40 lakh transactions a quarter). The unit must be the thing the outcome metric attaches to.

Name the one metric impact is measured against. Impact is not general goodness; it is a multiplier on a specific outcome. At Nihaar that outcome was renewal value per outlet. A team that scores impact against "customer delight" will produce numbers that cannot be checked afterwards, which quietly converts RICE back into advocacy with decimals.

Estimate effort as total delivery cost. Person-months across design, engineering, data, documentation, support enablement and, in Nihaar's case, hardware certification. Teams that count only engineering systematically over-rank work with long tails of migration and training.

Score in a room, then record the assumption behind each number. Sana Kabir, Nihaar's product analyst, kept a column called "because" beside each estimate. This column, not the score, is what the method is really for.

4. The worked example

Rau's team scored five finalists on 15 October. The window was the December quarter; the reach unit was outlets; impact was scored against renewal value per outlet using Intercom's conventional scale (3 = massive, 2 = high, 1 = medium, 0.5 = low, 0.25 = minimal); confidence used three rungs (100% for something measured, 80% for something with partial evidence, 50% for an argued case).

The arithmetic is worth doing by hand once. GST reconciliation: 5,800 × 0.5 = 2,900; × 1.00 = 2,900; ÷ 3 = 966.7. Printer certification: 2,300 × 1 = 2,300; × 0.80 = 1,840; ÷ 2 = 920. Note what has already happened. The two items that generated no argument at all — a dull compliance fix and a hardware certification — came first and second, because both touch enormous numbers of outlets for very little effort. The two items the executives had been fighting about came third and fourth. This is a common and instructive result: RICE tends to surface cheap broad work that nobody champions, because champions attach themselves to ambitious narrow work.

Then Kabir attacked the inputs. Offline billing's reach of 1,200 had come from Menon's pipeline, but the outlets that actually suffer outages severe enough to stop billing were, in Nihaar's own connectivity telemetry, 340 — the rest had four-hour battery-backed routers. Printer certification had been scored at 80 per cent confidence, but the external test lab's queue made the December window genuinely uncertain, so it fell to 50. That is the most important property of the method, and it is worth stating bluntly: the ranking is a function of the assumptions, and one bad assumption can move an item four places. A team that treats the output as an answer has misused it. A team that treats the output as a map of where its assumptions are load-bearing has used it exactly as intended.

5. Nuances a learner must acquire

Reach is a count in a window, not a market size

The commonest corruption is to write down the total addressable population because it is the largest defensible number. Reach should answer: in this window, how many units will actually encounter this change and have the opportunity to behave differently? For a feature buried three menus deep and used by 4 per cent of outlets, reach is 4 per cent of outlets, not all of them.

Impact is a multiplier on one named metric

The 3/2/1/0.5/0.25 scale is deliberately coarse because it is a judgement, not a measurement. Its discipline comes entirely from the metric being named. "Impact 2" means "roughly twice the per-unit effect on renewal value that a typical medium improvement produces". Without the metric, it means "I like this".

Confidence is about the other three numbers, not about shipping

Learners routinely discount confidence because the build is technically risky. That risk belongs in effort, as a wider estimate, or in a spike that reduces it. Confidence answers: how much evidence sits behind my reach and impact claims? A 50 per cent score means "this is an argued case with no data behind it", and the honest response is usually to go get the data rather than to ship on 50.

The score compresses; small gaps are noise

Given inputs on a five-rung impact scale and three-rung confidence scale, differences of less than roughly 20–30 per cent between two scores carry no information. Rau's convention was to band the list into tiers rather than read it as a strict ordering: anything within a quarter of the leader was in the same conversation.

The denominator assumes divisibility that does not exist

A score is a rate, which implicitly assumes you can buy fractions of items and that any person-month is interchangeable. Neither is true. Eight person-months of returns automation may be four calendar months of one squad that cannot be split, and the certification work may require the one engineer who also owns the payments integration. RICE ranks; it does not schedule.

It has no time dimension, and therefore no cost of delay

RICE cannot represent the fact that a GST schema change has a statutory date, or that a competitor's launch in March makes February work worth more than April work. Anything whose value decays or expires must be handled outside the score — most teams carry a small set of "must land by" items that bypass ranking entirely, and say so openly.

Strategic and platform work scores badly, predictably

Work whose payoff is a capability rather than an outcome — a data model refactor, a permissions system, an entry into a new segment — has low reach in the window and low confidence, and lands near the bottom every time. This is not a flaw to be argued away with inflated numbers; it is the method telling you truthfully that it cannot see options value. The correct response is to ring-fence a share of capacity for it, not to fake the inputs.

Scores are produced by people with interests

Once RICE decides budgets, estimates become negotiating positions. The tell is impact inflation: over two quarters, the share of items scored 2 or 3 rises. The countermeasures are structural — a single scorer or scoring pair for the whole list, effort estimated by the delivering team rather than the advocate, and a quarterly look back at whether last quarter's impact-2 items actually produced impact-2 outcomes.

6. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products, reach is abundant and cheap to measure but impact is treacherous: a change that reaches 40 lakh sessions at Neeharika Play, a regional streaming service, might shift completion rate by a fraction of a percentage point, so the sensible unit of impact is a measured delta from an experiment, and RICE becomes a pre-experiment triage device rather than a decision rule.

In B2B, the reverse holds. Reach is small, knowable and heavily skewed — at Nihaar, eleven chains represent 38 per cent of revenue — which means unweighted outlet counts can be actively misleading. Serious B2B teams weight reach by account value or segment, and must then be careful not to double-count value that is already inside the impact term.

In marketplaces, the trap is that reach has two sides. A change at Neelima Bazaar that reaches 12,000 sellers may reach zero buyers directly and yet move buyer conversion through supply quality. Scoring the seller side alone understates it; scoring both sides in one number hides which side the bet is on. The usual fix is to score the constrained side and note the other in the "because" column.

Stage matters too. At an early-stage company with one squad, the denominator dominates so completely that RICE degenerates into "do the cheap thing", and the more useful discipline is picking one hypothesis and testing it. RICE earns its keep from roughly three teams upward, where the list is long, the advocates are many, and the cost of an unreconstructable decision is high. At large companies the risk inverts: the score becomes an institution, gets a governance forum, and starts consuming more judgement than it produces.

7. Common mistakes

Scoring items that are not comparable. The symptom is a list mixing "add a column to the returns report" with "enter quick-commerce". The misunderstanding is that RICE compares options; in fact it compares options of similar granularity, because effort estimates for large items are wrong by multiples and the denominator swamps everything. Cheapest diagnostic: look at the spread of effort. If the largest item is more than about eight times the smallest, split or separate.

Using RICE to justify a decision already taken. The symptom is a score produced after the roadmap. The misunderstanding is treating the number as evidence rather than as a record of assumptions. Diagnostic: ask the scorer which input they would need to be wrong about for the item to drop out of the top five. If they cannot answer in one sentence, the score is decoration.

Letting effort be estimated by the advocate. The symptom is unusually round, unusually small denominators on the sponsor's pet item. Diagnostic: have the delivering engineer restate effort independently, before seeing the sponsor's number, and compare.

Reading the ordering too precisely. The symptom is a meeting spent arguing whether item four or item five goes first. Diagnostic: perturb one input by one rung and see whether the ordering survives. If it does not, the two items are tied and the choice should be made on grounds RICE cannot see — sequencing, team fit, or strategic commitment.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Rau's meeting takes ninety minutes and produces four artefacts: a scored list with a stated window and reach unit; a "because" column that a stranger could audit; a short list of the three assumptions the ranking is most sensitive to, with an owner and a date for checking each; and an explicit statement of what was decided outside the score — the compliance item that must land whatever it scores, and the 15 per cent of capacity reserved for platform work. Nobody says "the model chose". Someone says "we chose, and here is the number we would have to be wrong about".

9. What Rau decided

Nihaar shipped the GST reconciliation fixes and the printer certification, because both were cheap and broad and one of them was time-boxed by an external schedule. Returns automation went in at reduced scope: the two return types that made up 71 per cent of Nair's tickets, four person-months rather than eight, which lifted its score to 410 and changed the argument from "should we" to "how much". Offline billing was not built. Instead, Kabir was given three weeks and a survey of the twelve named chains to test whether the 340-outlet telemetry figure or Menon's 1,200 was closer to the truth — a ₹6 lakh question answered for perhaps ₹1 lakh of analyst time. Menon did not get his feature, but he got a date and a test, which is a materially different outcome from being overruled.

What to learn next follows directly from what RICE could not do here. Prioritising under constraints handles the sequencing and dependency problems that the divisibility assumption hides. Cost of delay supplies the time dimension the formula lacks. ICE and confidence calibration takes the weakest term — the one number in RICE that is a guess about guesses — and asks how you would know whether your 80 per cent means anything. And strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation addresses the structural bias against capability work, by allocating capacity to themes before items are scored at all.

Two questions to sit with. First: if your team's RICE ranking were re-run by a competitor's product team using their own estimates, which of your four terms would differ most — and what does that tell you about which term is actually doing the work? Second: what would you have to observe, three months after shipping, to conclude that an item you scored "impact 2" deserved a 0.5 — and is anyone at your company in a position to observe it?

RICE scoring, in depth

The formula is arithmetic anyone can do. What separates practitioners is knowing what the arithmetic assumes, how much of the answer is noise, and which decisions it is structurally unable to make.

1. Two rooms, the same week

On 6 January 2026, Ira Bhagat sat in a glass room in Lower Parel with a list of forty-one items and a quarter that had capacity for eleven. Bhagat was Head of Product at Nivriti Money, a Mumbai consumer investing app with 62 lakh registered users, 14.8 lakh monthly actives, and a business model that made almost nothing on any single user — so that the only lever that mattered was how many users moved from a single lump-sum purchase to a recurring monthly instruction. The company had spent the previous quarter shipping nineteen items and had moved that conversion rate by 0.3 percentage points. Her CEO's question at the December review had been unpleasantly precise: "Were those the wrong nineteen, or is nineteen just the wrong way to work?"

Four days later and 150 kilometres away, Karan Doshi convened a similar meeting in Pune with a very different list. Doshi was Director of Product at Neelotpal Health Systems, whose hospital information system ran the admissions, pharmacy and operating-theatre scheduling of 90 hospitals, 41,000 clinician users and ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue. Two of his customers — a 900-bed group and a chain of day-care surgical centres — together accounted for ₹19 crore, and both had escalated the same complaint about theatre scheduling. Meanwhile his largest count of users, the nursing staff across 74 smaller hospitals, wanted handover notes on a phone. Doshi had six squads and a renewal cycle that clustered in April.

Both had adopted RICE. Both had lists with scores on them. And both were about to discover that the scores were not the hard part. Bhagat's problem was that her scores were computed on reach figures taken from the top of funnels rather than the step being changed. Doshi's problem was more fundamental: his two candidate items could not be ranked at all until he decided whether "reach" at Neelotpal meant clinicians or revenue — and that single definitional choice, not any estimate in the sheet, determined the answer.

2. The idea, its history, and the camps that disagree about it

RICE scores a candidate piece of work as Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort. Reach is a count of units — users, accounts, sessions, outlets, clinicians — that will encounter the change inside a declared time window. Impact is a coarse multiplier, conventionally 3 (massive), 2 (high), 1 (medium), 0.5 (low), 0.25 (minimal), applied per unit reached and measured against one named outcome metric. Confidence is a percentage discount, conventionally 100, 80 or 50, expressing how much evidence stands behind the reach and impact estimates. Effort is total delivery cost in person-months across every function that must work, not engineering alone. The quotient has the units of expected outcome per person-month: a rate, a density, not a total.

The method was developed at Intercom around 2016 by Sean McBride and published on the company's product blog; it spread with unusual speed for an internal heuristic, largely because it was a modest, honest improvement on something almost every team already did badly. The predecessor is the value-versus-effort two-by-two, which asks a team to place items on a grid with "value" on one axis. The problem with that grid is not that it is wrong but that "value" is a single word doing four jobs, and two people who disagree about where an item sits cannot locate their disagreement. RICE's contribution is decomposition: it refuses the word value and splits it into how many, how much each, and how sure — three quantities that can be argued about separately and, crucially, checked separately afterwards.

The intellectual move is not the division. It is the insistence that a disagreement about priority must resolve into a disagreement about a named quantity.

Four camps hold genuinely different positions about what this buys you, and it is worth stating exactly what each would and would not sign.

The instrumentalists, closest to the method's origin, hold that a RICE score is a conversation device whose entire value is the argument it structures. They would sign: "scoring makes assumptions explicit and auditable." They would not sign: "the highest-scoring item should ship." For them, a team that stops arguing after the score is produced has destroyed the instrument.

The calibrationists, drawing on the decision-analysis tradition associated with Douglas Hubbard and on forecasting-tournament research, hold that point estimates are the disease and coarse scales make it worse. They would sign: "estimate in ranges, track whether your 80 per cent confidences are right 80 per cent of the time, and propagate the uncertainty." They would not sign: "a five-rung impact scale is good enough because it is only for ranking." Their evidence is that unmeasured estimators are systematically overconfident and that calibration is trainable.

The flow economists, following Donald Reinertsen's work on product development flow and its descendants in weighted-shortest-job-first, hold that any prioritisation without a time dimension is economically incoherent. They would sign: "the correct ordering is cost of delay divided by duration." They would not sign: "reach times impact captures the economic value of a decision." Their evidence is that in most product portfolios the cost of being late dominates the cost of building, and RICE cannot represent lateness at all.

The outcome school, associated with empowered-team thinking, holds that prioritising a feature backlog is itself the error — that teams should be handed problems and outcomes, not ranked lists of solutions. They would sign: "scored backlogs institutionalise the feature factory." They would not sign: "a ranked list is a legitimate output of good product work." Their evidence is the observed correlation between heavy backlog governance and organisations that ship constantly without moving metrics.

These are not four flavours of the same view. The flow economists and the instrumentalists disagree about whether the formula is missing a term or missing a purpose. The calibrationists think the arithmetic is fine and the inputs are worthless; the outcome school thinks the inputs may be fine and the arithmetic is beside the point. A practitioner who cannot state which camp a given objection comes from will mediate these arguments badly.

3. Mechanics in depth

The steps expert practitioners actually perform, in order, include several that never appear in the published description.

Declare the window, and understand what it privileges. Reach without a period is undefined. A quarterly window systematically favours items whose audience is present on day one and penalises items whose audience accumulates — a change that only new customers see at onboarding has a quarter's worth of new customers as its reach, which for a mature enterprise product may be almost nothing, even though the item may be the highest-leverage thing on the list over three years. The window must be identical across the list, and stated.

Declare the unit of reach, and recognise it as a strategic choice. Doshi's two options — clinicians or revenue-at-risk — are not two ways of measuring the same thing. Counting users treats a nurse in a 40-bed hospital and a surgeon in a 900-bed group as equal; counting revenue treats them as unequal by a factor of thirty. Neither is right in the abstract. The unit should be whatever the outcome metric attaches to, and if the outcome metric is net revenue retention, then the unit is money and everyone should say so out loud.

Place reach at the step being changed, not at the top of the funnel. This is the single most common technical error in practice. Bhagat's team had scored a rework of the recurring-instruction setup flow with a reach of 340,000 — the number of users who opened the investing tab in a quarter. The number of users who actually reached the failing authentication step was 61,000. The correction is a factor of 5.6 and it is not a judgement call; it is a query.

Name the outcome metric that impact multiplies. Impact of 2 must mean "roughly twice the per-unit effect on this named metric that a typical medium improvement produces". Without the metric named on the sheet, impact silently becomes an enthusiasm rating, and the historical check — did the impact-2 items actually behave like impact-2 items? — becomes impossible.

Estimate effort independently of the advocate. Total person-months across product, design, engineering, data, documentation, support enablement and any external dependency such as a certification lab or a partner bank's sandbox. Teams that count engineering only systematically over-rank work with long migration and training tails.

The quantitative treatment: where the noise lives

Because RICE is purely multiplicative, it is natural to analyse it in logarithms. Writing S for the score, log S = log R + log I + log C − log E. Errors that are multiplicative in the original terms become additive in log space, and if we treat the four estimation errors as roughly independent, the variance of log S is the sum of the four variances. This permits a genuinely useful calculation.

Suppose, plausibly, that a competent team's reach figure is good to about ±20 per cent, that impact is good to about one rung on the scale (a factor of two, since the rungs run 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3), that confidence is good to about ±30 per cent, and that effort estimates carry the classical software spread of about ±50 per cent. The table below propagates these.

Two conclusions follow, and both are load-bearing for everything that comes after. First, a RICE score is accurate to within a factor of roughly two and a half, which means that two items scoring 400 and 900 are not reliably distinguishable and two items scoring 400 and 4,000 clearly are. The method separates tiers, not positions. A team that spends a meeting arguing whether item six or item seven goes first is arguing about noise. Second, about two-thirds of that noise comes from the impact term — the one number in the formula that is a pure judgement on a coarse scale. Every hour spent refining reach queries while impact remains a show of hands is an hour spent polishing the least important term.

The second-order effects nobody mentions

Three structural properties of the formula have consequences that only show up after a few quarters of use.

First, multiplying by confidence makes RICE an expected-value engine, and expected value is risk-neutral. Multiplying a value estimate by a probability is only correct if the complementary outcome is worth exactly zero — that is, if a 50 per cent confident item is a coin flip between the full estimated value and nothing. Real product bets are not shaped like this. A speculative item often has a long tail: it usually returns little but occasionally returns ten times the estimate, and the knowledge gained from failure has value too. Multiplying by 0.5 destroys precisely the asymmetry that makes such bets worth taking as a portfolio. RICE is therefore structurally hostile to option-shaped work, and no amount of careful scoring fixes it.

Second, ordering by value-per-effort is the greedy solution to a fractional knapsack problem. That is a real result and it is why the method feels right: if capacity is a knapsack and items are divisible, greedy density ordering is provably optimal. But product items are not divisible; this is a 0/1 knapsack, where greedy is an approximation, and once items have precedence constraints — B cannot start until A ships — it becomes a precedence-constrained knapsack, for which greedy ordering can be arbitrarily far from optimal. A concrete case: a platform item scoring 120 that halves the effort of three later items scoring 600 each will never be selected by RICE, and its omission will quietly make the following two quarters more expensive.

Third, the denominator invites optimisation. Because the score rises as effort falls, any team whose budget is set by scores learns, without anyone intending it, that the reliable way to win is to make items smaller. Over several quarters this produces a backlog of cheap, broad, shallow items and a company that ships constantly and moves nothing.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

RICE earns its keep when four conditions hold, and each can be checked rather than assumed.

Claim one: the items are of comparable granularity. Test: the largest effort estimate on the list is less than about eight times the smallest. At Nivriti this held — everything was between two and nine person-months. At Neelotpal it did not: a theatre-scheduling rebuild at 24 person-months sat on the same sheet as a report column at 0.5, and the denominator swamped every other term. Doshi's list needed splitting before it needed scoring.

Claim two: one outcome metric genuinely dominates the period. Test: can you name it, and would the CEO name the same one? Bhagat could — recurring-instruction conversion. Doshi could not, because his quarter served both renewal risk in two large accounts and a product-led motion in small ones, which are different metrics with different units.

Claim three: value does not expire inside the window. Test: is there any item on the list with an external date? A statutory reporting change, a partner's API deprecation, an examination season, a festival peak. Every such item is invisible to the formula and must be handled before scoring, not inside it.

Claim four: the estimates are produced by people who do not benefit from the outcome. Test: who wrote the effort number? If the answer is "the sponsor", the score is advocacy in a lab coat.

Where RICE is actively misleading, as opposed to merely unhelpful, is a shorter and more important list: portfolios dominated by option-shaped bets, since risk-neutral discounting destroys the asymmetry; roadmaps with heavy precedence structure, since greedy ordering starves enabling work; and organisations where scores allocate budget, since the estimates then become negotiating positions and the measurement destroys the thing it measures.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies. Reach units differ across products — outlets here, clinicians there, sessions elsewhere — so scores are not comparable across product lines, however tempting the single sorted sheet looks. Mature companies do not solve this by normalising; they allocate capacity to products first, on strategic and financial grounds, and score only within each allocation. What they say in public is that they run one prioritisation process. What they actually run is a portfolio decision followed by several local ones.

Two-sided marketplaces. Reach exists on both sides and the sides are coupled. A change that reaches 12,000 sellers and no buyers may move buyer conversion through supply quality, with a lag. Scoring only the side you touch understates the item; summing both sides into one reach number hides which side the bet is on and makes the estimate unfalsifiable. The workable convention is to score reach on the constrained side of the market — whichever side is scarce this quarter — and to record the cross-side hypothesis explicitly as the reason for the impact rung.

Regulated products. In lending, insurance, health records and payments, a statutory item has infinite score and no score simultaneously: it must ship regardless. Treating compliance as a scored competitor is a category error, and the predictable organisational consequence is that the compliance function learns to inflate reach and impact in order to enter a process it should never have been in. The honest handling is a capacity tax taken off the top, sized and named, with the remainder scored.

Hardware plus software. Effort stops behaving like a divisible denominator when it contains a tooling freeze, a certification lead time or a bill-of-materials decision. Nishad Instruments, which builds connected diagnostic devices, found that its firmware items had effort distributions with a long right tail driven entirely by external test-lab queues, so the mean was a fiction and the median a worse one. Their adaptation was to score only the software-side items and to run hardware on a date-driven plan alongside — two processes, honestly separated.

AI-native products. Two terms break at once. Effort is bimodal: a retrieval feature is either three weeks or five months depending on whether the first evaluation run clears the bar, and nothing before that run distinguishes the cases. And confidence conflates two different uncertainties that need separating — whether the model can do the task at acceptable quality, and whether users want the task done. Nidhivan AI, which builds document-extraction software for logistics firms, split confidence into a technical rung and a demand rung and multiplied them, on the argument that a 70 per cent chance of the model working and a 70 per cent chance of anyone caring is a 49 per cent item, not a 70 per cent one.

Organisational seams. When several squads score into one list, effort inflation differs by squad, and the squad with the most conservative estimator is quietly defunded. Platform teams suffer worse: their reach is other teams, so either you count the end users of the dependent products — double-counting them against the product teams' own items — or you count the four squads served, which produces a reach of four. Neither is right, which is why mature companies ring-fence platform capacity rather than score it.

6. Nuances that separate experts from competent practitioners

Reach is a query, impact is a judgement — and they must be treated differently

The tell is a sheet where reach is a round number. Experts write reach as a query result with a date and a definition, and treat disagreement about it as an analytics task with a turnaround time. Impact, by contrast, will never be a query before the fact, so the expert's move is to make it falsifiable afterwards instead: record what an impact-2 outcome would look like in the metric, and check.

The confidence term is not a risk register

The obvious reading is that confidence captures "how likely is this to go well". The expert's reading is narrower: confidence discounts the reach and impact estimates only. Technical delivery risk belongs in effort, as a wider range or a de-risking spike. The tell is a sheet where the items with the newest technology all have 50 per cent confidence — a sign that the team has smuggled build risk into the numerator and will now under-invest in exactly the work that needs a spike.

A score of 50 per cent confidence is usually an instruction, not an estimate

Experts read a 50 next to a large numerator as a signal that the cheapest next action is research, not construction. If an item would rank first at 100 per cent confidence and eleventh at 50, then the value of resolving the uncertainty is the difference between those two allocations, and that is almost always larger than the cost of a two-week study. Competent practitioners score the item and move on; experts score the item and then price the experiment.

Impact rungs are ratios, so the scale spans a factor of twelve

From 0.25 to 3 is twelve-fold. Practitioners who think of the scale as "five options" underestimate how violent a single-rung change is; as the error propagation showed, one rung is a factor of two and dominates the noise budget. The expert's habit is to argue impact rungs hardest and longest, and to accept reach figures that are roughly right.

The list's shape reveals the organisation more than the scores do

An expert glances at the distribution before reading any individual score. If most items are between one and three person-months, the team is being defunded from structural work by its own process. If most items score within a factor of two of each other, the list has no information in it and the real constraint is elsewhere — probably capacity or clarity of strategy, not selection.

Rankings are stable at the extremes and random in the middle

Resample any realistic sheet within its uncertainty bands and the top two or three items stay top, the bottom third stays bottom, and the middle shuffles freely. The expert therefore extracts only what the method reliably provides — a tier assignment — and settles intra-tier order on grounds RICE cannot see: sequencing, team context, learning value, commitments already made to customers.

Scoring changes behaviour the moment it allocates money

The early warning is a drift in the distribution of impact rungs across quarters: the share of items scored 2 or 3 creeps up while outcomes do not. The expert's countermeasures are structural rather than exhortative — a single scoring pair for the whole list, effort estimated by the delivering team before they see the sponsor's number, and a published look-back comparing predicted and realised impact.

The method cannot price learning, and pretending otherwise is worse than admitting it

An experiment that will cost two person-months and reach 4,000 users has a terrible RICE score, because its direct impact is near zero; its value is the information it produces about ten other items. Experts do not try to encode this as a large impact rung. They take the honest route: a separate, ring-fenced learning allocation, defended on portfolio grounds, that does not compete in the same sheet.

Effort estimated in person-months hides the calendar

Twelve person-months can be three squad-months or twelve, and the difference decides whether an item lands before a renewal cycle. The tell is a roadmap whose RICE order and whose delivery order differ without anyone noticing. Experts score in person-months, then sequence in calendar time as a separate step, and treat any divergence between the two as something to explain rather than hide.

The best use of the sheet is as a historical record

Almost nobody does this, and it is where the compounding sits. A team that keeps four quarters of scored sheets can ask whether its 80 per cent confidences were right about 80 per cent of the time, whether its effort estimates were biased low by a consistent factor, and whether items scored impact 2 outperformed items scored impact 1. Those three questions turn an estimation ritual into an instrument that improves.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products, reach is large, cheap to query and reliable, so the weak term is impact, and the mature adaptation is to treat RICE as pre-experiment triage: score to decide what to test, then replace the impact rung with a measured lift for anything that matters. At Nivriti, the honest version of the sheet had two columns — an impact guess for untested items and a measured delta for anything that had run.

In B2B and enterprise the position reverses. Reach is small, knowable and violently skewed, so unweighted counts mislead, and the standard adaptation is to weight reach by account value or segment. The trap is double counting: if you weight reach by revenue and also score impact against revenue retention, the same economics appears twice and large accounts win everything. Neelotpal's discipline was to weight reach by ARR and score impact against clinician time saved, keeping the two terms in different units.

Platforms and marketplaces have the two-sided problem described above, and in addition a timing problem: supply-side improvements pay off on the demand side one or two cohorts later, which a quarterly window cannot see. Hardware, as noted, breaks the denominator's continuity. For AI products, effort is the least predictable term in any of these product types, and the useful adaptation is to score a cheap evaluation harness as its own item and re-score the rest afterwards.

Where the difference is often asserted but is not real: the terms themselves do not change meaning across these types. Reach is still a count in a window, impact is still a per-unit multiplier on a named metric. What changes is which term carries the error, and therefore where the argument should be spent.

By stage, the pattern is a curve rather than a line. In a company with one or two squads, the denominator dominates so completely that RICE degenerates into "do the cheap thing", and a single well-chosen hypothesis beats any ranking. Between roughly three and twenty squads the method is at its most valuable: the list is long, the advocates are many, and the cost of an unreconstructable decision is high. Above that, scores acquire a governance forum, a template and a compliance function of their own, and the marginal judgement produced falls below the judgement consumed — at which point large firms typically push scoring down into teams and replace the central sheet with capacity allocation against themes.

8. Three worked examples

Nivriti Money: the funnel-position correction

Nimish Bazaar: four quarters of the denominator death spiral

Nimish Bazaar, a Surat-based business-to-business marketplace for textile wholesalers, adopted RICE in April 2024 with unusual rigour: every item scored, capacity allocated strictly in score order, no exceptions. Over four quarters the results looked excellent on every process measure. Items shipped rose from 23 to 61 per quarter. Median effort per shipped item fell from 4.1 to 1.3 person-months. Seller satisfaction rose nine points. And gross merchandise value per active seller did not move at all — ₹3.9 lakh per quarter in April 2024, ₹3.9 lakh in March 2025 — while take rate stayed flat and the two structural items on the backlog, a credit-underwriting integration and a logistics rate engine, were scored in all four quarters and selected in none.

The failure was not in any estimate. It was that strict score ordering, applied without a floor, is an algorithm for shrinking work. Each quarter the cheapest broad items won; each quarter the structural items, whose reach in a single window was small and whose confidence was 50 per cent, lost by an order of magnitude. The recovery, run from April 2025, had three parts: a capacity split of 60 per cent to run-the-business items, 25 per cent to growth bets and 15 per cent to structural work, with scoring applied only within each bucket; an effort floor, so that anything under half a person-month left the sheet entirely and was funded from a standing maintenance allowance rather than competing; and a rule that any item scored below the line in three consecutive quarters had to be either killed explicitly or promoted to the structural bucket, so that permanent losers stopped absorbing scoring effort. By the December 2025 quarter, GMV per active seller was ₹4.3 lakh, up 11 per cent, and both structural items had shipped.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Denominator drift. Early sign: median effort per shipped item falling quarter on quarter while outcome metrics stay flat. Diagnostic question: what is the largest item we have shipped in the last two quarters, and would it have passed our own scoring? Cost of catching it late: at Nimish Bazaar, roughly a year of engineering capacity and a structural position in credit that a competitor took first.

Impact inflation. Early sign: the proportion of items scored 2 or 3 rising above about a third of the list. Diagnostic: pull last year's impact-2 items and ask what happened to the named metric. Cost of catching it late: the scores become uninformative, the process is quietly abandoned, and the organisation loses the audit trail that made decisions reviewable.

Reach taken from the top of the funnel. Early sign: reach figures that are round and identical across several items. Diagnostic: for each item, name the specific event in the product that constitutes "reached", and ask analytics to count it. Cost of catching it late: whole quarters spent on features whose real audience was a fifth of the one assumed — Bhagat's case, caught in time.

Compliance and platform work entering as competitors. Early sign: a statutory item with a suspiciously high impact rung, or a platform team quoting end-user reach. Diagnostic: ask whether the item would ship even if it scored last. If yes, it should not be in the sheet. Cost of catching it late: either a missed regulatory date or a corrupted scale that everyone stops believing.

Precision theatre. Early sign: meetings spent on the order of items five through nine. Diagnostic: perturb one impact rung on each and see whether the order survives. Cost of catching it late: mostly leadership hours, but also the slow erosion of the team's belief that prioritisation is a serious activity.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Three live disagreements deserve to be stated in their strongest form rather than harmonised.

Does the confidence term belong at all? The case for keeping it: uncertainty is real, and a method that ignores it will systematically over-fund speculative work by people who are good at telling stories; discounting by evidence quality is a cheap corrective that works. The case against: multiplying by probability imposes risk neutrality on a portfolio that should be deliberately convex, and in practice the 50 per cent rung becomes a place to park anything unfamiliar, so the term operates as a conservatism ratchet. For the sceptics to be wrong, you would need to observe organisations using confidence discounts that still fund a healthy share of option-shaped work — which does happen, but only where a separate learning budget exists, which rather concedes the point.

Is the absence of a time term a gap or a scope decision? The flow economists argue it is a gap that makes the method economically incoherent: if two items differ only in that one loses half its value by March, any ordering that ranks them equally is wrong, and cost of delay divided by duration is the correct form. The instrumentalist reply is that RICE was never meant to be an economic optimiser, that cost-of-delay estimates are far softer than they look — they require a value curve over time that almost no team can construct honestly — and that a simple method used well beats a sophisticated one used theatrically. For the flow position to be wrong, you would need cost-of-delay estimates to be so unreliable that adding them makes rankings worse; the honest state of the evidence is that this depends almost entirely on whether real external dates exist in the portfolio.

Should a feature backlog be ranked at all? The outcome school's steelman is not a preference for vagueness: it is the observation that a ranked list of solutions locks in the solution space before the problem is understood, that the teams which move metrics tend to be given outcomes rather than lists, and that scoring rituals give leadership the comfortable sensation of allocating capital while the actual product decisions are made upstream by whoever wrote the items. The steelman on the other side is that outcomes must eventually become work, that most organisations above a few hundred people cannot function without a legible allocation mechanism, and that an explicit, auditable one is better than an implicit one driven by whoever is most senior in the room. For the outcome school to be wrong, it would have to be true that empowered teams reliably self-coordinate across dependencies at scale — a claim with far less evidence behind it than its advocates usually admit.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised RICE rather than merely studied it behaves differently in four observable ways. They spend their argument budget on the impact rung and the reach definition, and accept the other two terms quickly, because they know where the variance lives. They read the output as tiers and say so out loud, refusing to litigate positions inside a tier. They are explicit about what sits outside the sheet — the statutory tax, the platform allocation, the learning budget — and they defend those allocations on portfolio grounds rather than smuggling them in with inflated numbers. And they keep the sheets, so that a year later they can say whether their own 80 per cent meant anything. The person who has merely studied it produces a beautifully formatted list, defends it as objective, and cannot tell you which single assumption, if wrong, would change the top three.

12. What each protagonist decided

Bhagat re-scored her list with reach defined at the step being changed rather than the funnel top, which moved seven of the forty-one items by more than a tier. She then cut the quarter's commitments from nineteen items to seven, took the reduced-scope recurring-instruction fix first, and reserved two person-months for a measurement harness that would let the following quarter's impact rungs be replaced by observed lifts. Her answer to her CEO was that nineteen had indeed been the wrong way to work, but that the deeper error had been scoring reach from the wrong place in the funnel for two years.

Doshi did not resolve his list in the January meeting. He took the reach-unit question to his executive team as what it was — a choice between defending a concentrated enterprise book and building a broad clinical product — obtained a decision to weight by revenue-at-risk for the coming two quarters given the April renewal cluster, and only then re-scored. The theatre-scheduling upgrade went first. He also split his list into two sheets by size, because a 24-person-month rebuild and a half-person-month report column had never belonged on the same page.

Discussion questions.

1. Neelotpal's ranking flipped on the definition of the reach unit while every estimate stayed constant. Where else in your own prioritisation does a definitional choice, made once and never revisited, silently decide outcomes that look like analysis?

2. Nimish Bazaar's process was followed faithfully for four quarters and produced a year of motion without progress. What is the minimum instrumentation that would have caught it by the second quarter, and who in the organisation would have had the standing to raise it?

3. Given that roughly two-thirds of the variance in a RICE score comes from a single coarse impact rung, is the right response to refine the impact scale, to replace it with measured experiment lifts, or to stop treating the output as a ranking at all? What does your answer imply about how much prioritisation effort is worth buying?

13. Going deeper

Value vs effort. The ancestor RICE decomposes; understanding what the two-by-two could and could not express tells you exactly what each of the three numerator terms was added to fix.

Prioritising under constraints. Handles what the ratio cannot: dependencies, sequencing, skill-specific capacity and the difference between person-months and calendar months. This is where the knapsack analogy stops being a metaphor.

Strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation. The structural answer to the denominator death spiral — allocate capacity to themes before items compete, so that enabling and structural work never has to win a fight it is built to lose.

ICE and confidence calibration. Takes the weakest term in the formula and asks the question that makes it real: when you say 80 per cent, are you right eight times in ten? Calibration is trainable, and it is the cheapest available upgrade to any scoring method.

Kano model. Supplies what impact rungs flatten: the difference between a feature that delights, one that satisfies proportionally, and one whose absence alone is felt. Table-stakes items are precisely the ones RICE scores badly.

Weighted scoring and WSJF. The generalisation and the rival. Weighted scoring lets you add criteria RICE omits; WSJF replaces the numerator with cost of delay and the denominator with duration, putting time where RICE has none.

Buy-a-feature. A different mechanism for the same problem — eliciting relative value from stakeholders or customers under a budget constraint, which sidesteps estimation bias by making people spend rather than score.

User story mapping. Addresses the granularity precondition directly: a map gives you a principled way to slice large items into comparable ones so that the effort spread on your sheet stays inside the range where scoring works.

Saying no. The organisational skill without which any scoring method becomes decorative, because a list with nothing below the line is not a prioritisation.

Cost of delay. The missing time dimension, treated properly: how to construct a value-over-time curve, when the effort of doing so pays for itself, and why most portfolios contain only a handful of items where it changes the answer.

Parchoon Retail Networks: The Slate That Would Not Add Up

A distribution-technology company in Pune must publish an eighteen-month product plan on Monday morning. The scoring sheet that is supposed to produce it ranks nine initiatives in an order that nobody in the room believes and that the company cannot legally follow.

1. Sunday night, Baner

Pune, Sunday 14 February 2027, 10.40 p.m. Nandita Kulkarni, Chief Product Officer of Parchoon Retail Networks, had the planning workbook open on one screen and, on the other, the slide she was expected to present at nine the next morning: a single ranked list of the nine initiatives that would consume the company's engineering capacity from April 2027 to March 2028. The summit was an internal ritual: thirty people in the Baner office and eleven on a bridge from Bengaluru, Gurugram, Kolkata, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore and New Jersey. The board meeting that mattered was Thursday, and behind it sat a Series D term sheet that Harish Menon, the co-founder and chief executive, expected in March, conditioned on a credible eighteen-month plan.

Parchoon had used RICE scoring for eleven quarters. Every initiative owner submitted a reach figure, an impact rating on the standard 0.25-to-3 scale, a confidence percentage and an effort estimate in engineering person-weeks; product operations combined them and published the ranking; the ranking set the roadmap. The process had survived two reorganisations and had kept the company out of the founder-whim school of planning. Nandita had defended it in three board meetings and once to a distributor in Rajkot who wanted to know why his route-planning request had waited four quarters.

The sheet in front of her now (Exhibit 1) put a predictive reordering feature for the free retailer app at the top with a score of 2,178, twice the next item. It put the platform rewrite that four other initiatives depended on at zero, because the rewrite reached no users directly. It put the Dubai enterprise rollout — which Parchoon was contractually obliged to deliver by 30 April 2027, with liquidated damages written into the statement of work — seventh of nine. And a compliance build that the company had no choice about at all sat second, not because anyone had judged it important but because the Digital Personal Data Protection Act applied to every registered user, and eleven lakh people in the reach column will outvote almost anything.

Funding the ranking in order consumed 990 of the 1,100 discretionary person-weeks available in the first half and left the Dubai contract unfunded. Nandita had run that arithmetic four times. What she had instead was a framework that had produced, with perfect internal consistency, a plan that was commercially reckless and technically impossible.

2. How Parchoon got here

Parchoon Retail Networks was founded in Pune in 2018 by Harish Menon, who had spent fourteen years in FMCG general trade sales across Kerala and Maharashtra, and Sarthak Bose, an engineer from Kolkata. Their observation was ordinary and correct: India's roughly one crore twenty lakh kirana stores were served by a fragmented layer of distributors running on paper, WhatsApp and unlicensed billing software, and the order a retailer placed with a salesman on a Tuesday morning was invisible to everyone upstream.

Parchoon built two products. Parchoon Dukaan is a free Android application through which a retailer orders from the distributors already serving that pin code; by January 2027 it had 11.42 lakh registered retailers and an annualised GMV of about ₹9,800 crore, monetised through a 0.4 per cent take rate charged to distributors and brand-funded promotions. Parchoon Vitaran is the paid distributor management system — stock, schemes, claims, beat plans, GST-compliant invoicing — licensed to 1,420 distributor businesses at an average ₹6.9 lakh a year. FY27 revenue was tracking at ₹228 crore against ₹174 crore, at 61 per cent gross margin and an EBITDA loss of ₹38 crore, with ₹186 crore of cash left from a ₹320 crore Series C raised in August 2025.

Two earlier decisions constrain everything on Nandita's desk. The first was made in September 2022, when the GST e-invoicing threshold came down and Parchoon's distributor customers needed IRN generation inside eleven weeks or they would stop being able to bill. Bose chose to put the invoicing and ledger logic into the existing shared schema that already served Dukaan, on the reasoning — sound at the time — that a single ledger was the only way to ship in eleven weeks. Parchoon shipped in nine. The consequence, four and a half years later, is that the retailer app and the distributor SaaS share one transactional core: a change to scheme calculation for a dairy distributor in Erode touches code paths serving a paan shop in Patna, and every estimate for either product silently includes the cost of not breaking the other. Bose left in late 2024. The second decision came in April 2025, when Parchoon tied 30 per cent of every lead's variable pay to initiatives shipped against plan — that is, to the outputs of the RICE sheet. Nobody proposed inflating scores. Scores rose anyway.

Prepared by the author from company records. The two decisions marked in darker type are the ones most frequently cited inside Parchoon as the reason a given estimate is what it is.

3. The industry

Parchoon competes on three fronts that behave nothing like each other. In retailer-facing commerce it sits alongside Udaan, ElasticRun, Jumbotail and Solv, and increasingly against JioMart's partner programme, while quick-commerce platforms — Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart — erode the kirana basket that Parchoon's retailers depend on for footfall. In distributor software it competes with Bizom, FieldAssist and a long tail of regional billing vendors whose advantage is an implementation partner who will come to the godown on a Sunday. And since 2024 it sells internationally: the Gulf grocery trade runs on a distributor structure recognisably similar to India's, and many of its storekeepers and route salesmen are Malayali and Tamil.

Regulation is not background here, it is product surface. GST e-invoicing and the reporting window on the invoice registration portal dictate release calendars; the RBI's digital lending directions govern anything Parchoon does with embedded credit; the DPDP Act's consent and retention obligations apply to eleven lakh retailers whose phone numbers Parchoon holds; ONDC's participation rules matter to whether Dukaan becomes a node or remains an island; FSSAI cold-chain norms shape the categories the Vitaran telemetry initiative addresses. Seasonality is equally concrete: the August-to-October stocking cycle running through Onam, Ganesh Chaturthi and Diwali is when distributors make their year, and Parchoon does not ship risky changes into it.

In June 2026 Parchoon signed its first large international customer, Bustan Retail Group, a Dubai-headquartered grocery and wholesale business operating 640 outlets across the UAE and Oman. The contract is worth ₹41 crore over three years, with ₹11 crore invoiced on go-live, a go-live date of 30 April 2027 and liquidated damages of 1.5 per cent of the annual fee for every week of delay, capped at 10 per cent.

4. The situation in detail

The FY28 planning cycle opened on 12 January 2027 with the same template Parchoon had used for eleven quarters. Nine initiatives were submitted by 29 January. Product operations published the ranking on 2 February, and it was on that day that the plan began to come apart, in four separate ways that each looked, at first, like a clerical problem.

The first was the ledger migration. Abhijit Sen, who took over engineering after Bose's exit, submitted an estimate of 620 person-weeks to separate the Dukaan and Vitaran transactional cores, and left the reach field blank: "Reach is every future initiative. There is no number that belongs here." Product operations, needing the sheet to compute, entered zero. The migration ranked ninth of nine with a score of zero, the arithmetic working exactly as specified.

The second was reach itself. Ritu Dhawan's smart-reorder initiative used 4.90 lakh, the thirty-day active retailer count from the warehouse. On 6 February, Rohit Chandrasekhar in Toronto circulated the reconciliation in Exhibit 4, observing that Parchoon has at least five defensible definitions of an active retailer, from 11.42 lakh down to 1.96 lakh. At 4.90 lakh the smart reorder scores 2,178 and leads comfortably; at the GSTIN-based count of 1.96 lakh it scores 871 and falls behind the DPDP consent build. Nobody had chosen the thirty-day definition dishonestly; it was the number that appeared on the growth dashboard.

The third was effort. In November 2026 the programme-management office compared estimated with actual person-weeks for twenty-three shipped initiatives (Exhibit 2). The growth pod came in at a median 1.15 times estimate, the Vitaran pod at 1.6, the platform pod at 2.9. Read one way, platform work is chronically underestimated and RICE has been quietly rewarding teams whose work is easiest to slice thinly. Read another way — and Abhijit read it this way, loudly — the platform sample is three projects, one of which absorbed remediation weeks from the November 2025 IRP outage, and correcting effort by a historical factor punishes exactly the team the framework already undercounts. Exhibit 3 applies the correction: the order barely moves, but the slate stops fitting altogether.

The fourth emerged on 11 February, when Serena Lim's team in Singapore established that Arabic right-to-left support, UAE VAT treatment and Omani entity handling could not be delivered on the existing shared schema without a multi-tenancy change that is, functionally, the first third of Abhijit's migration. Bustan had been scored as a 340-week initiative independent of the ledger work. It is not independent. Nobody had asked, because the template has no field for dependency.

There is a fifth thing, which Nandita has not put in the deck. In September 2026 Parchoon shipped a festive credit pilot with an NBFC partner, Adat Finserv, scored at 60 per cent confidence, which by the QBR's own accounting delivered 2.3 times its predicted impact. That success is one of the two points doing most of the work in Exhibit 5, the chart Farida Contractor uses to argue that RICE predicts outcomes well enough to run the company on. The realised-impact numbers in it were computed by the same people whose bonuses depended on them, against metric definitions that changed in April 2026.

5. The people

Nandita Kulkarni, Chief Product Officer, Pune. Owns the process and the Monday slide. Says the slate must be honest before it is optimised; her incentive is the Series D, since a plan the board trusts is worth more to her than any one initiative. What she does not say is that she introduced RICE at Parchoon in 2023 and would be dismantling her own credential by telling the summit that the ranking is not a decision.

Harish Menon, Co-founder and CEO, Pune. Wants the international story and the ONDC story both intact, because both are in the Series D deck. Says he will back whatever Nandita decides. What he does not say is that he has already told two prospective investors that Bustan goes live in April and that a second Gulf logo follows in FY28.

Farida Contractor, CFO, Mumbai. Wants RICE scores in the board pack as a capital-allocation discipline, and wants reach weighted by revenue per unit, which would put Vitaran and enterprise work above everything on Dukaan. Her incentive is a defensible burn story for the term sheet. What she does not say is that the ₹412 in Exhibit 6 uses a last-touch attribution her own team has flagged internally as unreliable.

Abhijit Sen, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Wants the ledger migration funded in full in the first half. Says that every quarter it is deferred adds roughly 15 per cent to every other estimate. His incentive is an engineering organisation that stops paying interest on a 2022 decision he did not make. What he does not say is that his 620-week estimate has a range he has never written down, and that he fears anchoring anyone on the lower end of it.

Ritu Dhawan, Head of Growth, Gurugram. Owns the smart reorder and the vernacular expansion, the two initiatives the ranking loves. Says growth work deserves its position because it is the only work with measurable reach. Her incentive is straightforward: 30 per cent of her variable pay tracks shipped initiatives, and her pod ships small things reliably. What she does not say is that she chose the thirty-day active count over the transacting count in an earlier cycle when both were available.

Annika Vogel, Principal Designer, Berlin. Owns the vernacular and accessibility work for Bangla, Tamil and Odia. Says the framework treats a first-time retailer in Cuttack who cannot read the app and a power user who wants one more button as the same unit of reach. What she does not say is that the 70 per cent confidence on her initiative rests on a fourteen-person study run in Kolkata in 2025.

Sopan Money: Ranking the Q3 Backlog

Bengaluru, 10 September 2026. Ananya Deshpande, VP of Product at Sopan Money, closed her laptop at half past nine and looked again at the spreadsheet she had promised the founders by Friday. In eight days, the company's quarterly business review would open with a single slide: the prioritised product roadmap for the October–December quarter, ranked, resourced, and defensible in front of a board that included two venture investors who asked pointed questions about capital efficiency. Seven initiatives sat in the backlog, each with a Reach, Impact, Confidence and Effort score that its owner had submitted the previous Monday. On paper, the ranking was already computed. Ananya's problem was that she no longer trusted the numbers that produced it.

Company background

Sopan Money was founded in 2017 by Rohan Kapadia and Neha Bhatt, two engineers who left a Bengaluru brokerage to build a direct mutual-fund and stock-investing app for India's first generation of app-native retail investors. The company is registered with SEBI as an investment adviser and with AMFI as a mutual-fund distributor, offers zero-commission direct plans, discount stock broking through a partner clearing member, the National Pension System, and digital gold, and completes know-your-customer checks through Aadhaar e-KYC and CKYC in line with RBI and DPDP Act requirements. By August 2026 the app had 18 lakh registered users, 4.3 lakh monthly active investors, and ₹3,400 crore in assets under management, growing but still a fraction of Groww's user base and well behind Zerodha's broking volumes; Paytm Money, Angel One and INDmoney compete for the same young, mobile-first investor. In 2024 Sopan opened a non-resident Indian product line, targeting the large Indian professional community in the Gulf, a corridor where INDmoney and the NRI desks of ICICI Direct and HDFC Securities were already active. At the July town hall, Rohan told the wider company, and later the board, that Sopan would "move aggressively" into the Gulf NRI market in the second half of the fiscal year.

The situation

Sopan's product organisation runs a lean quarterly process: each functional lead pitches one initiative with self-scored RICE inputs, Ananya's product-operations analyst compiles them into a single ranked list, and the top items are funded against the coming quarter's engineering capacity, roughly 26 person-weeks after 10 weeks are reserved for on-call support and compliance patches out of a 36-week pod. Seven pitches arrived this cycle, shown in Exhibit 1, and their combined effort request of 43 person-weeks was never going to fit. That was expected; the list existed to force a choice. What troubled Ananya, reading the sheet on Wednesday night, was how the numbers behind the choice had been produced. Every owner had rated their own initiative's confidence between 70 and 90 percent, regardless of how much evidence stood behind the number. Reach figures came from at least three different sources: Devika Iyer, the data scientist in Toronto who built the model behind the SIP-continuation nudge, had pulled hers from the funnel in Exhibit 3; others were estimates typed from memory. Two items exposed the sharpest gap between the score and the reality behind it. The Gulf NRI onboarding revamp, which Rohan had already promised the board, scored low on confidence because the market was genuinely unproven, and sat near the bottom of the raw ranking despite being, in effect, already decided. The Dubai corporate integration that Sanjay Mehta, the New Jersey-based head of sales and partnerships, had pitched carried a self-rated confidence of 85 percent, but when Ananya checked with legal on Wednesday morning, the client's contract was still unsigned, with no date promised before Diwali. From Pune, Karthik Rao, the engineering lead, had written to Ananya separately to say that whatever the sheet ranked, he wanted the redemption-latency fix funded, after three days in August when the market fell sharply, redemption requests queued for over four minutes, and support tickets spiked to nine times the daily average. From Berlin, Rahel Fischer, the lead product designer, had submitted her accessibility redesign late in Ananya's morning because of the nine-and-a-half-hour gap, with a note that reach-based scoring, in her view, systematically undercounted design and inclusion work whose benefit shows up gradually across many small interactions rather than in one visible spike.

The people

Karthik Rao, Engineering Lead, Pune. Owns the redemption-latency fix. Distrusts what he calls "spreadsheet politics" and wants reliability work judged on incident data, not on a reach number that, in his view, nobody can verify.

Rahel Fischer, Lead Product Designer, Berlin. Owns the accessible onboarding redesign. Argues that RICE, built around features with sharp, countable outcomes, structurally undervalues design and inclusion work, and wants her initiative judged on more than a five-week effort estimate.

Mei-Ling Tan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Owns the complaint-resolution flow. Holds the clearest evidence of the seven pitches, drawn directly from support tickets and Play Store reviews, and is the least worried that her confidence score will be challenged.

Sanjay Mehta, Head of Sales and Partnerships, New Jersey. Owns the Dubai corporate integration, a salary-linked SIP plan for a Gulf facilities conglomerate's roughly 4,800 India-origin staff. Needs engineering capacity reserved so the product is ready the week the contract is signed, and is frustrated that a framework built around millions of retail users makes his single enterprise deal look small.

Read together, the three exhibits make Ananya's problem concrete. Exhibit 1 ranks the SIP nudge model first by a wide margin, and Exhibit 3 shows why that number can be trusted: its reach traces directly to the bottom of a measured funnel. The Gulf revamp and the Dubai integration, by contrast, rest on estimates nobody in the funnel can confirm. Exhibit 2 shows what happens once confidence is judged against evidence rather than self-reported: the accessible redesign, which looked like the clear second choice, falls to a tie with the social feed once its 60 percent confidence is corrected to 30, while the redemption fix and the nudge model, both grounded in real incident and experiment data, rise. Two items barely move in relative terms no matter which sheet is read: the Gulf revamp, ranked low under both because the market genuinely is unproven, and the Dubai deal, ranked lowest under both because a single 4,800-person contract will never out-reach a retail feature.

The options

  1. Ship the self-reported ranking as submitted. Funding the top five items in Exhibit 1 within 26 weeks — the SIP nudge, the accessible redesign, the social feed, the complaint-resolution flow and the Gulf revamp — is fast, respects the process every lead already agreed to, and requires no confrontation before Friday. Its cost is that it locks in capacity on the strength of Rahel's self-rated 60 percent confidence, which Exhibit 2 suggests is closer to 30, and it drops both the redemption-latency fix, despite August's incident data, and the Dubai integration entirely, with no plan to revisit it.
  2. Pause and recalibrate every score against the evidence rubric, then rank strictly by the result. Exhibit 2's numbers are more honest and easier to defend to the board, and the recalibrated top five — the nudge model, the social feed, the accessible redesign, the complaint flow and the Gulf revamp — happen to protect the founders' public commitment. But the review itself would take Karthik, Rahel, Mei-Ling and Sanjay through a defensive re-justification of their numbers with only days left before the review, and it still excludes the redemption fix, because RICE, honestly scored, still treats a reliability problem as a modest-impact item rather than as risk avoided.
  3. Reserve capacity for the two commitments RICE cannot fairly price, and let recalibrated RICE govern the rest. Ananya carves out capacity up front for the Gulf revamp, run as a bounded pilot given its honestly low confidence, and for the redemption-latency fix, justified by the August incident rather than by its RICE score; she then uses Exhibit 2's recalibrated numbers to rank the SIP nudge, the complaint flow, the accessible redesign and the social feed for whatever capacity remains; and she gates the Dubai integration on a signed contract, deferring it to next quarter rather than scoring it into this one. The upside is a roadmap that is honest where RICE works and explicit where it does not. The cost is that Ananya must defend two overrides to the board and to the leads whose items lost ground because of them.

Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which initiatives fit inside 26 person-weeks if the self-reported numbers are trusted as given? What does the result reveal about how RICE rewards the way an input is estimated, not only the merit of the initiative behind it?
  2. Compare Exhibits 1 and 2. Which two initiatives move the most once confidence is judged against an evidence rubric rather than self-reported, and why does that gap matter more for some initiatives than others?
  3. Exhibit 3 shows where Sopan's most trustworthy reach number comes from. For each of the other six initiatives, what would you ask its owner before accepting their reach figure?
  4. RICE ranks the redemption-latency fix and the Dubai integration low under both Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, yet the company has reasons, outside the framework, to value both. Should Ananya override the ranking for these two, and if so, how does she keep that choice defensible rather than arbitrary?

A note for the learner

RICE is useful precisely because it forces four separate judgment calls — how many people an initiative reaches, how much it moves them, how sure you are, and what it costs — into the open, where they can be compared and challenged. It is a scoring convention, not a decision procedure, and it inherits whatever bias sits inside its inputs. A weak answer to this case treats Exhibit 1's ranking as a verdict and moves on. A well-reasoned answer notices two separate failure modes. First, self-reported confidence launders incentive into apparent objectivity: whoever is most fluent in the framework, or most invested in the outcome, tends to score their own initiative highest, which is exactly what happened with the accessible redesign and the Dubai integration. Recalibrating against evidence, as Exhibit 2 does, fixes this. Second, and more durably, RICE's reach term is built for features consumed in small increments by many users, so it structurally undercounts two kinds of work that do not look like that: reliability and risk work, whose benefit is a loss avoided rather than a visible gain, and a single concentrated enterprise relationship, whose value has nothing to do with how many people it "reaches." No amount of recalibration fixes this second problem, because it is not a measurement error; it is a mismatch between the shape of the initiative and the shape of the metric.

The defensible path is Option 3. Ananya should reserve capacity first for the Gulf revamp and the redemption-latency fix, on grounds she states explicitly and separately from their RICE scores — a public board commitment in one case, incident evidence in the other — and let the recalibrated numbers in Exhibit 2 govern the discretionary capacity that remains. The Dubai integration should be gated on a signed contract rather than scored into this quarter's roadmap at all. Written down alongside the ranking, this reads as a considered exception to a rule the team can otherwise trust, not as a favour to whoever argued loudest, and it leaves Sopan with a durable habit for future quarters: initiative owners defend their confidence against Devika's funnel and against incident data, not against their own optimism, and RICE is asked to do only the job it can do well.
